newsitem.title: UK: Britain's schools become pre-election battleground.
newsitem.headline: Britain's schools become pre-election battleground.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major left state school at 16 and worked his way up to lead a Conservative party run by an elite educated in exclusive private schools.

Tony Blair went to Fettes College, the select Edinburgh school, and then Oxford University -- the classic route to establishment power -- before taking control of a Labour party committed to equality in education.
Given this, it is hardly surprising the differences between Labour and the Conservatives on education have shrunk. But the issue will be a key battleground at the election.

"Increasingly Labour is trying to be as much like the Conservatives as they can," said Stephen Pollard, a former head of research at the Labour-affiliated Fabian Society think tank, who quit after a row over school policy.
Labour, attacking Conservative policy as "nostalgia for a return to an elitist excellence for a few (which) ignores the aspiration of the many", disputes this.
Labour leader Tony Blair vowed to make education his number one priority if, as polls suggest, he wins Britain's forthcoming election, now at most four months away.
Blair told BBC television he wanted to pursue education reform with the same vigour as former Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher overhauled Britain's union laws.
After 18 years in the political wilderness, Labour needs the middle class votes that have given the Conservatives four consecutive terms in office.
Shredding old dogmas in a drive to modernise Labour and win over the middle class, Blair dismayed traditional supporters by vowing not to kill off selective grammar schools.
In another U-turn, Blair agreed schools should have more control over their own affairs, an idea championed by Major.
Blair has pledged to sack substandard teachers, close poor schools, set minimum homework requirements and punish parents who fail to control their children.

And despite opposition to overall selection by ability at age 11, Labour under Blair now accepts streaming within schools in individual subjects -- a distinction some experts see as politically expedient rather than educationally significant.
"I...cannot see the difference between selection and specialisation," Pollard, now head of research at the centrist Social Market Foundation, told Reuters.

Blair's stance has won him possibly more enemies than in any other policy area; enemies who have homed in on his decision to send his son to a grant-maintained school -- which has opted out of local authority control -- rather than a comprehensive.
But Blair, who has said his children's future will not be sacrificed to political correctness, has faced them all down.
His political control did not waver when his social security spokeswoman, Harriet Harman, went even further and sent her son to a selective grant-maintained school.
Her open defiance of party policy against selection of pupils at 11 led to hundreds of Labour faithful sending back their membership cards. But Blair backed her and Harman stayed.
Labour's shift has left Major with a dilemma.

After almost a decade in which the government has introduced a national curriculum, begun national tests for children and encouraged schools to opt out of local authority control, the Conservatives are short of new ideas to fight back.
One of the government's new schemes -- nursery vouchers designed to counter Labour's plans for free nursery places for three and four year olds -- is having a shaky start.
The government watchdog, the Audit Commission, has warned the scheme will need careful monitoring to prevent fraud.
Fighting back, Major has pinpointed selection and parent choice as the defining issues between himself and Blair.

Overruling his Education Secretary, Gillian Shephard, who argued for consolidation after years of dramatic change, Major called for a "grammar school in every town" and for more schools to be able to select which pupils they take at 11.
But he immediately ran into fire from one of Britain's leading commentators on education, Sir Claus Moser, who said he was dismayed by Major's approach.
"It is all about politics, not about children. Labour policy statements are freer of political dogma," Moser, a former head of the government's statistical service, said last year.

But there was a sting in the tail. Moser said Labour would have to boost education spending by at least 3.0 billion pounds ($5.02 billion) a year to raise levels of literacy and numeracy. come from, I don't know," Smithers told Reuters.
